payload.content: The chaining-degrades-more-gracefully claim implicitly assumes simple uniform hashing (each key equally likely to land in any bucket, independent of others) — stated explicitly after Craig questioned it. Under that assumption chain lengths cluster tightly around the load factor (Poisson-ish), so long chains are rare in practice — but chaining has no structural cap on chain length: a bad or adversarial hash function (hash-flooding attacks) can put all n keys in one bucket, giving O(n) worst-case lookup. Open addressing has a structural cap chaining lacks: since each slot holds exactly one key, no lookup can ever need more than m probes (table size) — worst case is bounded regardless of hash function quality. Net correction: 'open addressing degrades faster than chaining at the same load factor' is an average-case claim conditioned on a reasonable hash function, not a worst-case guarantee — worst-case the ranking flips, since chaining's downside is unbounded (can exceed table size m) and open addressing's is not.

payload.content: Dynamic array amortized doubling — why append is "amortized O(1)" despite occasional O(n) resize-copies. Worked both growth strategies by hand over 16 appends (step-by-step tables) to ground the asymptotic claim in concrete arithmetic, then projected to n=64 to show the fixed-increment average climbing while doubling stayed flat. payload.content: Constant factors are dropped in Big-O -- O(log2 n) and O(log10 n) are the same class, differing only by a constant multiplier; convention uses base 2 because most log-time algorithms work by repeated halving. The halving mechanism: log_b(n) counts halvings, not items, so doubling n costs exactly one more step in log time versus n/2 more steps in linear time -- the actual mechanical reason logs are cheap. Best/worst/average case are a separate axis from growth-rate class; any of O(1)/O(log n)/O(n)/O(n^2) can carry any of the three. Unspecified Big-O defaults to worst case by convention, since it is the only guarantee that does not depend on assumptions about input distribution -- corrected from an initial average-case guess. Labeled best/worst/average breakdown of linear search (target at index 0 vs. index n-1/absent vs. uniformly distributed), worked as three short cases rather than one combined paragraph. payload.content: prev/data/next node structure -- the direct fix for the singly-linked deletion gotcha, since the predecessor is now reachable from the node itself. Cost of the fix: pointer overhead roughly doubles per node (8 vs. 16 bytes on a typical 64-bit system), and every splice touches more pointers -- 4 for insertion (new node's prev+next, plus each neighbor's one link), 2 for middle-node deletion -- corrected mid-session after Craig cross-checked the general claim against the worked diagram and found insertion and deletion were being conflated. Misconception flagged: doubly-linked fixes navigation direction and O(1) deletion-by-pointer, not random access -- indexed lookup is still O(n). Deps: Linked Lists. Contrasts: Linked Lists (singly vs. doubly).

questions.question: Say a team builds a "hybrid" mobile app -- not a full native app, just a thin wrapper that loads your website inside an embedded WebView (a browser window with no address bar). Would cookie-based session auth work the same way there as in a normal browser tab, or would it behave like a plain native app? Walk me through why.
questions.answer: Uncertain -- guessed cookies need to be stored in a browser's local cache and wasn't sure whether WebView has that option.
questions.feedback: Right instinct (it hinges on whether WebView has a cookie store) but no firm answer. Explained: a WebView is a full embedded browser engine (Chromium on Android, WebKit on iOS), so it carries the entire HTTP stack including the cookie jar -- cookie auto-attach works exactly like a normal tab. A plain native app has no such engine and makes raw network calls with no built-in cookie handling. This reframes the earlier 'closer to hardware' misconception (g62-1): it's not about hardware distance, it's about whether browser-engine code is present. Confirmed understood on follow-up.

questions.question: Say a site has a stored-XSS hole -- an attacker's script is running inside a logged-in user's page. The session cookie has HttpOnly and Secure set, but not SameSite. Can the attacker walk away with the cookie's actual value and reuse it later from their own machine? Can they still do damage while the script is running on the victim's page? Explain what's protected and what isn't, and why.
questions.answer: Correctly identified that the browser still auto-attaches the HttpOnly cookie to requests the injected script fires, so the attacker can act as the victim in the moment. Initially attributed a missing-SameSite scenario to the attacker being able to reuse the stolen cookie from their own machine later. Pushed back that this was really describing CSRF being possible without SameSite (a true statement) rather than theft-and-replay. Through discussion, correctly separated CSRF (blind -- the victim's own browser fires the forged request; the attacker never touches the cookie value) from theft-and-replay (governed entirely by HttpOnly, independent of SameSite), and concluded theft-and-replay specifically is not possible here because HttpOnly already blocks the script from reading the value.
questions.feedback: The hard part -- HttpOnly still lets the browser auto-attach the cookie to script-fired requests -- was right immediately. The gap: attributing cookie theft-and-replay to a missing SameSite flag. Corrected via the CSRF-is-blind framing (attacker never sees the value; it's the victim's own browser doing the work) vs. HttpOnly (the only thing governing whether the value can be read at all). Good-faith pushback with a real partial truth (missing SameSite does enable CSRF) led to a clean, fully self-derived final answer.

questions.question: You're choosing between session-based auth and JWTs for a new API behind a load balancer in front of 50 backend instances, and policy requires revoking a compromised credential within seconds. Which fits, and what's the actual cost of going the other way?
questions.answer: Session-based auth, because validity is a live server-side lookup that can be flipped immediately. JWTs have no such lookup -- a compromised token stays valid until its own expiry (e.g. 3600s) regardless of policy, and that window is the real cost of choosing JWTs here.
questions.feedback: Correct and complete -- named the underlying mechanism (server-side record vs. self-contained token) and the exact cost (the expiry window as an exploitable gap) with no prompting needed.

gaps.text: Retest of g62-1 ('why mobile favors tokens'), via a fresh WebView scenario rather than the original question: initial answer was uncertain rather than firmly wrong (correctly guessed it depends on whether WebView has a cookie store, but couldn't confirm). Explained that a WebView is an embedded browser engine (Chromium/WebKit) carrying the full HTTP stack including the cookie jar, vs. a plain native app which has no browser engine and makes raw calls with no built-in cookie handling. Confirmed understood on follow-up. Worth a light confirm-only check next review rather than a full re-teach.

Fresh gap, surfaced on an HttpOnly/XSS scenario: conflated a missing SameSite flag with enabling the XSS attacker to steal-and-replay the cookie from their own machine. Corrected by separating CSRF (a blind forged request the victim's own browser fires and attaches the cookie to -- the attacker never sees the value) from theft-and-replay (governed entirely by HttpOnly, independent of SameSite). Craig pushed back with the legitimate observation that missing SameSite does enable CSRF, and from there correctly re-derived that theft-and-replay specifically was not possible in this scenario given HttpOnly was set. Worth a light confirm-only check next review.

resource.title: Software Testing Course – Playwright, E2E, and AI Agents

payload.content:
Software testing acts as an insurance policy for code quality, preventing high-stakes production failures like Knight Capital's $460M loss or Therac-25 radiation over-dosages.

1. The Testing Pyramid (Full-Stack Architecture Scope):
Balances speed, cost, and confidence across three layers:
- Unit Tests (Base): Highly isolated, fast (~milliseconds), test pure functions/components using mocks/stubs.
- Integration Tests (Middle): Medium speed/cost, test boundaries and communication between 2+ modules or systems (e.g., backend API to database).
- End-to-End (E2E) Tests (Peak): Slowest, highest cost and maintenance, test complete real-world user workflows in actual browser environments (e.g., via Playwright).

Worked Example (1,000 total tests for an e-commerce app):
- 800 Unit Tests (e.g., tax calculation logic): ~2 seconds total runtime.
- 150 Integration Tests (e.g., checkout service persisting orders to PostgreSQL): ~15 seconds total runtime.
- 50 E2E Tests (e.g., Playwright driving UI login, cart, and checkout flow): ~5–10 minutes total runtime.

ASCII Diagrams:
Unit Test:
[Input: $10] ---> ( calc_tax() ) ---> [Output: $1.50]

Integration Test:
( Checkout Service ) <===> ( PostgreSQL Database )

E2E Test:
[ Playwright Browser ] ---> ( Frontend UI ) ---> ( Backend API ) ---> ( Database )

The Testing Ice Cream Cone (Tempting-but-wrong alternative):
Developers rely heavily on slow E2E tests while skipping unit tests because unit tests use dummy data. Counterexample: 500 E2E tests taking 3 hours cause developers to stop running local test suites. When tests fail with generic UI timeout errors, debugging becomes a nightmare because E2E tests report symptoms across the entire system rather than pinpointing root code causes.

2. The UI Testing Ladder (Frontend UI Scope):
Organizes client-side quality by visual and interactive granularity:
- Level 1: UI Element Appearance (visual, styling, layout; tested via visual snapshot tools like Percy/Chromatic).
- Level 2: UI Element Behavior (component interactivity and state transitions in isolation; tested via React Testing Library/JSDOM).
- Level 3: User Journey Testing (multi-step workflow simulation; overlaps directly with E2E Testing).

Visual Rendering Blindspot:
Functional tests check DOM presence, not pixel reality (e.g., z-index: -1 or off-screen flex-wrap bugs pass DOM assertions). Bridged using Visual Regression Snapshot Testing (e.g., Playwright's toHaveScreenshot()).

3. Functional vs. Non-Functional Testing:
- Functional (Pyramid & UI Ladder): Verifies WHAT the system does.
- Non-Functional: Verifies HOW WELL the system performs under constraints (Load/Performance testing, Security/OWASP vulnerability scanning, Accessibility/a11y WCAG compliance, Chaos Engineering like Chaos Monkey).

4. Timeline Perspective (Shift-Left vs. Shift-Right):
- Shift-Left (Pre-Release): Catching bugs early in design/development (linters, static typing, TDD, automated PR tests).
- Shift-Right (Post-Release/Production): Testing live production systems (Canary releases, feature flags, synthetic monitoring, A/B testing).

5. Visibility Perspective:
- White-Box: Full code visibility (unit tests).
- Black-Box: Zero code visibility, testing purely against inputs/outputs (E2E browser tests).
- Gray-Box: Partial code visibility (e.g., testing external HTTP APIs while knowing the DB schema).

Connections:
Connects directly to Backend APIs (backend/apis), where contract testing and unit testing business logic in isolation keep slow E2E suites small and focused strictly on frontend wiring.
payload.notes: Pushed back on whether E2E tests give zero location info for bugs, correctly observing that Playwright logs and step traces pinpoint user-journey failure points, though root-cause code debugging still requires full-stack investigation. Explored mental models comparing the Testing Pyramid with the UI Testing Ladder, non-functional quality attributes, timeline shifts (shift-left/right), and code visibility levels.

questions.question: Imagine you are adding a new feature to the TechMart app: if a user has 5 or more items in their cart, they automatically get a 10% discount. You want to verify that this exact discount math works correctly. Based on the testing pyramid, which level of test (Unit, Integration, or E2E) should you use to verify this specific calculation, and what happens to your test suite if you decide to write an E2E test for this instead?
questions.answer: Use a unit test. Writing an E2E test instead introduces external failure points (network, UI, database), so if the test fails, it's ambiguous whether the discount logic or another system component broke.
questions.feedback: Correct! You accurately identified that a unit test is ideal for pure business logic, whereas an E2E test introduces extraneous failure modes that hide whether the discount math itself broke.

questions.question: Suppose your backend team renames a field in the JSON response for fetching cart items—changing "items" to "cart_items". The frontend unit tests pass (because they use dummy mock data with the old field name), and the backend unit tests pass (because the endpoint correctly returns JSON). Yet in production, the shopping cart page renders totally blank. What level of test was missing from your suite, and why did the individual unit tests fail to catch this bug?
questions.answer: An integration test was missing. Integration tests verify whether two independent modules work together correctly. Unit tests failed because they relied on outdated mock data that did not reflect the breaking JSON schema change.
questions.feedback: Correct! You correctly identified that an integration test checks the boundary where two components meet, which is precisely where mock-based unit tests fail because mocks hide breaking schema changes.

questions.question: Imagine your team uses Playwright to run an automated checkout test suite on every pull request. The test involves making a real HTTP call to a third-party payment gateway (like Stripe). In CI/CD, this test randomly fails 15% of the time because Stripe occasionally rate-limits the CI server or takes too long to respond. What strategy should you apply to your test suite to eliminate this flakiness without removing the checkout test entirely, and what potential risk do you take on by doing so?
questions.answer: Rely on the test running successfully at least once to prove payload validity, use detailed logging/monitoring to track rate-limiting or network issues, and run E2E tests, acknowledging that lack of unit tests makes pinpointing failures harder and increases execution time.
questions.feedback: Incorrect. To eliminate third-party API flakiness and rate limiting in CI/CD, the standard strategy is API Mocking (stubbing network responses, e.g. using Playwright's network interception to return a canned 200 OK response). Relying on real live calls plus logging still leaves CI/CD builds flaky and slow. The trade-off/risk of API mocking is schema drift: if Stripe changes its API contract or error responses in production, your mock won't detect the breakage.

gaps.text: Conflated handling third-party API flakiness in E2E/CI tests with retry/logging rather than using network mocking/stubbing, missing the trade-off of schema drift.

payload.notes: First two questions answered cleanly with solid understanding of unit and integration test boundaries. Question 3 revealed a misconception regarding handling third-party network dependencies in automated CI/CD pipelines.

payload.content:
WHY MEMORY EXISTS. An LLM is stateless: each call sees only its context window. "Memory" is the system that decides what goes into that window on each turn. Stuffing the whole history in fails on cost, latency and accuracy: in the Hindsight paper a 20B model given the full conversation history scored 39% on LongMemEval; the same model with a memory layer scored 83.6%.

THE FOUR-STAGE PIPELINE every memory system has:
  conversation --> [1 WRITE: extract facts] --> [2 STORE] --> [3 READ: retrieve + assemble] --> context window
                                                     ^
                                         [4 MAINTAIN: update / merge / forget]
Stage 4 is the hard one. It is cache invalidation again (see State & Caching): the problem is not finding a fact, it is knowing that a fact has stopped being true.

TEMPTING-BUT-WRONG: plain RAG over chat logs (chunk, embed, top-k by cosine similarity). Counterexample: in March the user says "I work at Google"; in June, "I just started at Stripe as a PM". Asked "where does Alex work?", similarity search returns both chunks, possibly Google first because the wording matches better. RAG has no idea of which fact is current. It also fails multi-hop questions ("book a table in my sister's city on her birthday" needs two facts that never appear together).

THREE DESIGNS, one per approach to "knowledge changes over time":

1) SUPERMEMORY — a graph of extracted facts, built for fast personalization. Documents (raw PDFs, chats, URLs) are kept separate from memories (facts extracted from them). Memories link by three relations: UPDATES (the new fact replaces the old; "Alex at Stripe" UPDATES "Alex at Google"; the old one is kept for history, and an isLatest flag makes search return only the current one), EXTENDS (adds detail without invalidating: "leads a team of 5" extends "PM at Stripe"), DERIVES (inferred from several memories: "likely works on core payments"). Forgetting is built in: time-based decay for temporary facts, newer-wins contradiction handling, filtering out casual chatter. Keeps a static + dynamic user profile always in context. Claims sub-400ms retrieval.

2) ZEP / GRAPHITI — a temporal knowledge graph. Entities are nodes and facts are edges. Bi-temporal: every edge records two timelines, when it was true in the world (valid / invalid) and when the system learned or retired it (created / expired). Example: edge Alex -WORKS_AT-> Google, valid 2023 .. invalid 2026-06. The edge is closed, not deleted, so "where did Alex work in 2024?" is answerable. Three layers: episodes (raw messages, kept as provenance), the entity graph, and communities (clusters of entities with summaries). Retrieval combines cosine similarity, BM25 keyword search and graph traversal (breadth-first search), then reranks. Reported: 94.8% vs MemGPT's 93.4% on DMR; on LongMemEval, up to +18.5% accuracy and about 90% lower latency than full-context.

3) HINDSIGHT (Vectorize, open source, Dec 2025) — separates memories by epistemic type into four networks: World (objective facts), Experience (what the agent itself did, first person), Opinion (judgements stored with a confidence between 0 and 1 and a timestamp; confidence goes up with supporting evidence and down with contradicting evidence) and Observation (neutral entity summaries built from many facts). Three operations: RETAIN (turn transcripts into facts with time ranges, canonical entities and links), RECALL (four parallel channels: semantic vectors, BM25 keywords, graph spreading activation, temporal filter; fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion; reranked by a cross-encoder; cut to a token budget), REFLECT (answer, and form or update opinions). Reported LongMemEval: 39% full-context baseline -> 83.6% (same 20B model) -> 91.4% (larger backbone). LoCoMo: prior best open system 75.78% -> 85.67% / 89.61%.

WORKED EXAMPLE — Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = sum over channels of 1/(60 + rank). Fact A is rank 1 in vector search and rank 3 in BM25: 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0164 + 0.0159 = 0.0323. Fact B is rank 2 in vector search and missing from BM25: 1/62 = 0.0161. A wins because two independent channels agree. RRF uses ranks, not raw scores, so a cosine score of 0.83 and a BM25 score of 14.2 never have to be put on the same scale.

MAP OF THE FIELD (two axes):
 Representation: flat vector store (LangMem, early Mem0) -> fact graph with versions (Supermemory, Mem0 graph) -> temporal knowledge graph (Zep) -> typed epistemic networks (Hindsight). A separate line is OS-style tiers (Letta/MemGPT: core memory always in context, recall memory, archival memory), where the agent pages memory in and out itself.
 Who decides what gets written: a background extraction pipeline (Supermemory, Zep, Hindsight) vs the agent calling memory tools itself (Letta; file-based memory like CLAUDE.md or a memory tool writing markdown files).
 Convergence: nearly every serious system now does hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword + graph + time) followed by reranking. The designs differ on what gets stored and how it gets updated, not on how it gets searched.

BENCHMARKS AND THE CAVEAT: LongMemEval (500 questions testing information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention) and LoCoMo are the standard tests. Scores are mostly self-reported and swing with the backbone LLM: Hindsight itself moves from 83.6% to 91.4% just by swapping the model. A Vectorize comparison lists Hindsight 94.6%, Supermemory 81.6%, Zep 63.8% and Mem0 49%, but Vectorize makes Hindsight, and Zep reports its own numbers differently. Both benchmarks test recall from conversations, not whether an agent gets better at its job over time.

COUNTERINTUITIVE: (1) retrieval is mostly a solved problem; updating is the hard part. (2) Forgetting is a feature. (3) The backbone model can move the score as much as the memory architecture does.

WHERE EACH WINS: Supermemory for a consumer chat app that needs fast "who is this user" context; Zep for enterprise or support agents where "what was true when" matters (a customer's plan history, compliance audits); Hindsight for long-running agents that have to form and revise judgements (a research or trading assistant).

CONNECTIONS: Database Fundamentals (these are databases with LLM-driven writes; bi-temporal tables come from SQL:2011); State & Caching (memory update = cache invalidation; recency decay is like an eviction policy); Hash Tables (entity canonicalization, resolving "Alex" / "Alex D." to one key).

Sources used: Hindsight paper arXiv 2512.12818; Zep paper arXiv 2501.13956; supermemory.ai/docs/concepts/graph-memory and blog/memory-engine; vectorize.io comparison (vendor-authored). Forward pointers (beyond current depth): embeddings & ANN indexes (HNSW), BM25 internals, cross-encoder rerankers, knowledge-graph modelling, Letta/MemGPT self-editing memory in depth, memory for learning-from-experience (procedural memory). Connection to Craig's own plan: the SWE book as shared state for many agents is itself a file-based memory system.

questions.question: Reading app: each book row stores author_name directly (no authors table) so a 50-book home feed loads fast. An author with 40 books changes her pen name. (a) Normalized or denormalized, and what did it buy? (b) What goes wrong/gets expensive on the rename, and how would the normalized design handle it? (c) Is denormalization 'a NoSQL thing'?
questions.answer: Denormalized; buys read speed (no author lookup/join). Rename means updating all 40 book rows; normalized = one row in an authors table keyed by id. Denormalization is NoSQL's default but a relational table can be denormalized too.
questions.feedback: Correct on all three. Added: besides cost, the rename risks an update anomaly - if one of the 40 updates fails or misses a row (e.g. a book inserted mid-rename with the old name), some books show the old name and some the new. A single source of truth makes that impossible.

questions.question: Concert tickets: booking logic in one transaction at Repeatable Read is (1) SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE concert_id=7, (2) if sold < 500, INSERT a ticket. 499 sold; two buyers click Buy simultaneously. (a) Walk through what can happen; which anomaly (dirty / non-repeatable / phantom) is it, and why doesn't Repeatable Read necessarily stop it? (b) Two fixes: one that changes isolation level, one that doesn't.
questions.answer: Understood the business problem (overselling) but said the isolation-level theory was fuzzy; did not attempt, asked to revise it after the quiz.
questions.feedback: Deferred to the revision session at Craig's request. (Intended answer: both read 499, both insert -> 501 tickets. It's a phantom-style anomaly (write skew): each transaction's check is invalidated by a NEW row the other inserts, and Repeatable Read only protects rows already read, not rows that don't exist yet. Fixes: Serializable isolation; or without changing level - lock a parent row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the concert row), keep a seats_sold counter with a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE sold < 500, or a unique constraint on (concert_id, seat_no).)

questions.question: One leader + two async replicas; writes go to the leader, reads to a random replica. A user saves a new profile bio, the page reloads and shows the OLD bio; 10s later a refresh shows the new one. (a) Explain step by step. (b) Two ways to stop the user seeing their own stale data without making the whole system synchronous, with the cost of each.
questions.answer: (a) Write hit the leader; the immediate reload read a replica that hadn't received the change yet; 10s later it had. (b) Only offered optimistic UI updates (cost: false impression if the write fails, extra verification). Couldn't name a second method.
questions.feedback: (a) exactly right. (b) Optimistic updates only cover the moment after Save - a page reload wipes client state, re-queries the server, lands on a lagging replica and shows the old bio again; also fails on another tab/device. The property needed is read-your-writes consistency, fixed server-side: (1) route this user's reads to the leader for a short window (e.g. 15s) after they write - cost: extra leader load, which is what replicas were meant to offload; variant: reads of your OWN profile go to the leader, others' profiles to replicas, since users only notice staleness in what they just changed. (2) Track replication position: the leader numbers every change (e.g. write #10,482); remember the user's last write position (cookie/session) and only read from a replica that has applied at least that position, else wait or fall back to the leader - cost: complexity and occasional slower reads.

questions.question: A messaging app shards its messages table by sender user_id across 8 shards. (a) Loading all messages between a user and a friend in time order - what must the database layer do and why is it slower than one machine? (b) A better shard key for this access pattern, and one query that gets WORSE under the new key.
questions.answer: (a) Fetch from the shards holding each user's messages, aggregate, sort by time (initially said all shards, corrected to two). (b) Shard by conversation_id so a whole conversation lives on one shard; after a follow-up prompt: 'all messages a user sent' gets worse because they spread across many conversations/shards.
questions.feedback: Correct. Refinements: it's 2 shards not 8 - the router knows both user_ids; it's slower because of two network round-trips, waiting on the slower shard, and merge-sorting in the application instead of one indexed ordered read. A query lacking the shard key (full-text search) would hit all 8. Every shard key makes one grouping cheap and scatters all others - also 'delete my account and all my messages' or a per-user inbox of latest messages.

questions.question: Two regions (Mumbai, Singapore) replicating to each other; the link drops for 3 minutes. (a) Shopping cart: during the partition a user adds a book in Mumbai and removes a pen in Singapore from another device. CP or AP? What does the cart look like after healing and what reconciliation strategy fits? (b) Flight seat booking: seat 14C is free and two users in different regions both try to book it during the partition. CP or AP? What does the user in the 'losing' region see during those 3 minutes?
questions.answer: Did not attempt - said he doesn't know what CP and AP mean; asked to flag as a gap and revise.
questions.feedback: Deferred to the revision session. (Intended answer: (a) AP - a cart should always accept edits; after healing, merge both sides (union of adds, apply removes) -> book added AND pen removed; last-write-wins would lose one edit. (b) CP - selling one seat twice is unacceptable; the region that can't confirm with the other refuses or holds the booking ('try again shortly' / pending) until the link heals, i.e. unavailable for those 3 minutes.)

gaps.text: Isolation levels and phantom reads: can't explain why Repeatable Read doesn't stop a count-then-insert race (write skew / phantom) or name the fixes (Serializable, row lock via SELECT FOR UPDATE, conditional update, unique constraint).

Read-your-writes consistency under async replication: only knew client-side optimistic updates; didn't know server-side fixes (route recent writers' reads to the leader, track replication position/LSN per user).
CAP theorem: doesn't recall what CP vs AP mean or how to choose between them per use case (cart = AP with merge, seat booking = CP).

resource.title: Understanding Deep Learning (Prince), Ch 3: Shallow neural networks

payload.content:
A shallow neural network is linear regression with hinges added. Linear regression y = phi0 + phi1*x has two knobs (height, slope) and can only draw a straight line. Adding lines together never helps: (1 + 2x) + (3 - x) = 4 + x is still a line. Something must bend each line before they are summed.

ReLU is the bending tool: negatives become 0, positives pass through unchanged (ReLU(-7) = 0, ReLU(4) = 4). A line passed through ReLU becomes a hockey stick: flat at zero, then rising from the point where the line crossed zero. That point is a hinge ("joint"). Everyday example: an auto fare of Rs 30 for the first 2 km then Rs 15/km is 30 + 15*ReLU(km - 2); at 1 km -> Rs 30, at 6 km -> Rs 90. That is a one-hinge network, which linear regression cannot express.

Equation 3.1 decoded with a slab electricity tariff (fixed charge Rs 50; Rs 3/unit to 100 units, Rs 6/unit 100-300, Rs 9/unit above 300 - each slab adds Rs 3/unit):
  h1 = ReLU(0 + 1x), h2 = ReLU(-100 + 1x), h3 = ReLU(-300 + 1x)
  bill = 50 + 3*h1 + 3*h2 + 3*h3
At 250 units: h1 = 250, h2 = 150, h3 = 0 -> bill = 50 + 750 + 450 = Rs 1,250, matching the slab calculation.

Symbols: theta_d0 = intercept of hidden unit d's line (hinge sits at x = -theta_d0/theta_d1); theta_d1 = its slope; a[.] = activation (ReLU); h1..h3 = hidden units; phi1..phi3 = how much each hinge changes the slope; phi0 = overall height. Subscripts read "which hidden unit, then 0 for intercept or 1 for slope". Ten knobs instead of Chapter 2's two; training is unchanged (least-squares loss, search for the knob values that minimise it).

Vocabulary: a hidden unit is active past its hinge and inactive when clipped to zero. The slope of any region = sum of the slope contributions of the active units (tariff above 300 units: 3 + 3 + 3 = Rs 9/unit - slope vs slope CHANGE is a common trap). D hidden units -> at most D hinges -> at most D + 1 straight pieces. Negative weights let the curve bend downward, so a network can rise, fall and rise again.

"Only three of the four slopes are independent" (3.1.1): give each unit one number c_d, its slope contribution when active. Every region's slope is a sum of the c's of the active units, so four region slopes come from three numbers and the fourth is forced. If all units switch on to the right, the leftmost region has no active units and its slope is 0. If some units face left (negative theta slope), the forced slope is instead a sum of other regions' slopes - e.g. hinges at 1, 2, 3 with c = 2, -1 (left-facing), 3 give slopes -1, 1, 2, 5, and 1 = -1 + 2. Practical meaning: three units can't draw four unrelated slopes; you need a fourth unit.

Multiple inputs: with 2 inputs each hinge becomes a line across the map; the lines cut the map into polygons, and over each polygon the output is a flat tilted plane (a faceted gemstone over terrain). Multiple outputs share the hidden units, so every output can only bend at the same joints (a zero weight can remove a bend from one output).

Universal approximation (3.2): with enough hidden units a shallow network can approximate any continuous function on a bounded range as closely as wanted - more, shorter straight pieces, like a many-sided polygon approximating a circle. It is an existence result: no bound on units, no promise training finds the settings, no promise of good predictions on new data.

questions.question: Suppose you delete every ReLU from a shallow network, so each hidden unit passes its line straight through. What shapes can the network draw now, and why? What does that tell you about ReLU's job?
questions.answer: Declined to guess - not yet clear on the role of ReLU.
questions.feedback: Without ReLU the network can only draw a straight line: a weighted sum of lines is a line. Worked example: units 2x - 4 and -x + 6, output = unit1 + 3*unit2 = -x + 14 (x=1 -> 13, 3 -> 11, 7 -> 7, slope -1 everywhere). With ReLU: x=1 -> 0 + 3*5 = 15, x=3 -> 2 + 3*3 = 11, x=7 -> 10 + 0 = 10; slope -2 then -0.25, so the line bends. ReLU's one job is to put a bend into each hidden unit's line; without it, any number of hidden units collapses back to linear regression.

questions.question: A network has 1 input, 1 output and 5 ReLU hidden units, trained on 1,000 points shaped like a smooth hill. What is the most straight pieces its fitted curve can have, what will the fit look like, and what changes with 50 hidden units?
questions.answer: Six linear regions; a six-segment piecewise-linear approximation of the hill; with 50 units the pieces get short enough to closely approximate the smooth hill.
questions.feedback: Correct. 'Up to' six: if two hinges coincide or a unit's weight is zero, there are fewer pieces.

questions.question: Now the network takes 2 inputs (latitude and longitude) and predicts terrain elevation. In the 1-input case each hinge was a point on the x-axis. What does each hinge become on the 2D map, and what do the flat pieces of the output surface look like?
questions.answer: Each hinge becomes a line; the flat pieces are polygons.
questions.feedback: Correct. The hinge lines cut the map into polygon patches; over each patch the elevation surface is a flat tilted plane.

questions.question: A network has 1 input, 3 hidden units and 2 outputs (price and demand). The price output bends at x = 2, 5 and 8. Where can the demand output bend, and why?
questions.answer: Also at 2, 5 and 8, because the same hidden units feed both outputs and the hidden units determine where the bends are.
questions.feedback: Correct and well reasoned. Demand CAN bend only there, but may not bend at all three: a zero weight on a hidden unit removes that bend from demand's curve.

questions.question: The universal approximation theorem says a shallow network can approximate any continuous function. Name what it promises, and at least two things it does not promise that matter in practice.
questions.answer: Declined to guess.
questions.feedback: It promises that some shallow network with enough hidden units can match any continuous function on a bounded range as closely as wanted. It does NOT promise: how many units are needed (could be millions); that training will find the right settings (a route exists, no map); that the network will predict well on new data.

gaps.text: Role of ReLU: without an activation, sums of lines stay a line no matter how many units; ReLU is what adds the bends.
Universal approximation is an existence result: no bound on units, no guarantee training finds the network, no guarantee of generalisation.

payload.notes: 3/5. Craig chose not to guess on Q1 and Q5, which pinpointed the two gaps.

payload.content:
What a neural network is for: a general-purpose shape-maker that approximates almost any relationship between inputs and outputs. Two refinements to the 'any squiggle, any 3D object' picture:
1. A network is a function - each input gives exactly one output - so a 1-input/1-output network cannot draw a loop. Workaround via output choice: input = time, outputs = (x position, y position) traces a path that can loop and cross itself.
2. Terrain fits directly (2 inputs lat/lon -> 1 output elevation), but overhangs, caves or a coffee mug have two heights at one map point. Fix by asking a different question: input a 3D point, output signed distance to the surface (positive outside, negative inside); the object is where the output is zero. Used in neural graphics.
In practice the 'shape' is usually invisible: a 224x224 colour image is about 150,000 input numbers, and the network builds a faceted surface in 150,000 dimensions.

Why it works splits in two: (a) why it CAN represent almost anything - ReLU hinges glue flat pieces together (universal approximation); (b) why it actually works on real problems - how training finds good settings (UDL Ch 6-7) and why fitting training data generalises to new data (Ch 8-9, and partly still open, Ch 20).

Choosing inputs and outputs: for images, audio and video the input is usually the raw numbers the data is made of; the output defines the task.
- Images: pixels scaled to 0-1, 224*224*3 = 150,528 numbers. Outputs: class scores (1,000 for ImageNet), boxes + labels, or one label per pixel (e.g. satellite land-cover maps).
- Audio: raw samples (16,000/s -> 160,000 numbers for 10 s) or a spectrogram (80 bands x 100 steps/s -> 80,000 numbers for 10 s). Outputs: transcript, speaker, next chunk of sound.
- Video: stacks of frames (16 frames of 224x224 colour ~ 2.4 million numbers). Outputs: action label, caption, next frame.
- Self-supervision: make the output the next piece of the data itself (next frame, next word) so data labels itself - how large language models are trained.
- Raw pixels into a fully connected shallow network is impractical: 150,528 inputs x 1,000 hidden units = ~150 million first-layer weights; convolutional networks (Ch 10) redesign the wiring.
payload.notes: Craig's own framing ('networks model almost any function; I see what they can do but not yet why they work') was refined, not corrected.

questions.question: A colleague builds a network with 3 hidden layers of 500 units each but forgets any activation function. They train it on the smooth-hill data. What will the fitted curve look like, and why didn't 1,500 hidden units help?
questions.answer: Without activations each unit computes a line; summing lines gives a line, so layer 1 passes lines to layer 2, which again only has lines, and so on. The output is a straight line regardless of depth or width; only the activation creates bends.
questions.feedback: Correct - a line fed into a line is a line (layer 1: 3x + 1; layer 2: 2*(that) + 4 = 6x + 6). The result is the best straight line through the data, i.e. Chapter 2's linear regression - for a symmetric hill, a nearly flat line at the hill's average height.

questions.question: Someone says: 'The universal approximation theorem proves that a shallow network with 100 hidden units, trained on my 500 house-price records, will accurately predict prices for new houses.' Name at least three problems with this claim.
questions.answer: The theorem gives no bound on how many hidden units are needed; it says nothing about whether training will find the network; and it makes no claim the learned model generalises beyond the 500 records - it only says such a network exists.
questions.feedback: Correct on all three. Sharpening: the theorem concerns approximating the true function, while 500 noisy records are only a sample of it - mixing up 'the function' with 'my data' is another face of the generalisation problem (Ch 8). 'Existence result' is the standard name.

resource.title: Understanding Deep Learning (Prince), Ch 4: Deep neural networks

payload.content:
Why stack layers instead of widening one: a wider layer ADDS hinges (D units -> at most D + 1 pieces), a new layer MULTIPLIES them.

Folding (UDL 4.1): compose two 3-unit shallow networks. Set the first to zigzag: as x goes 0->1 y rises 0->1, 1->2 y falls back to 0, 2->3 y rises again. Three stretches of x all land on the same range of y - like folding a paper strip into a Z. The second network draws its own 3-piece pattern over y in [0,1]; because three stretches were folded onto that range, the pattern is drawn three times, once per stretch, and stretches that run backwards give mirrored copies. 3 x 3 = 9 pieces from 6 hidden units, versus at most 7 for one layer of 6. Nine units: one layer gives 10 pieces; three layers of 3 each folding 3 ways give 3 x 3 x 3 = 27.

The catch: the pieces are copies of one pattern, flipped and stretched, not free choices - the copies cannot be different patterns (one a bump, another a step). Depth wins when the target has repeated or reused structure (edges look alike anywhere in a photo; a syllable sounds similar in any word): early layers build a part once and later layers reuse it everywhere. With ReLU, a deep network still draws straight pieces joined at hinges; depth changes how many pieces you get per knob, not their kind. Real networks fold less neatly - training decides where and how much.
payload.notes: Taught with an interactive folding widget (fold 0-4 times; bump/step/tick patterns).

resource.title: Understanding Deep Learning (Prince), Ch 4: Deep neural networks

payload.content:
Equations 4.7-4.9 (two hidden layers, three units each). New letter psi ('sigh') names the layer-1 -> layer-2 knobs; theta = input -> layer 1, phi' = layer 2 -> output; a prime means 'second-layer version'. Every layer does the same three steps: multiply each input by a knob, add up plus an offset, clip with ReLU. Layer 1 units read one input (2 knobs each); layer 2 units read ALL layer-1 units (offset + 3 weights = 4 knobs each); the output is a weighted sum plus offset, unclipped. psi_23 = how much h'2 listens to h3 (first digit receiver, second digit source, 0 = offset). Knobs: 6 theta + 12 psi + 4 phi' = 22, versus 19 for a 6-unit shallow network.
Worked example, x = 2: layer 1 (offset, slope) = (-1,1), (1,-1), (-3,2) -> before ReLU 1, -1, 1 -> h = [1, 0, 1]. Layer 2 rows (offset; weights on h1,h2,h3): (0; 2,1,-1) -> 1; (-1; 1,3,1) -> 1; (2; -1,0,-3) -> -2 -> h' = [1, 1, 0]. Output: 0.5 + 2*1 + 1*1 + 4*0 = 3.5. An inactive unit (h2 = 0) is silent to the whole next layer. Renaming the composed products theta'*phi as free psi values is why a two-layer network is a broader family than two stacked shallow networks.

Matrix notation (4.4) adds no new maths. Vector = column of numbers; matrix = grid; matrix x vector = for each row, multiply item by item and add up - exactly each unit's recipe, one row per unit. 4.14 shorthand: h = a[theta0 + theta x], h' = a[psi0 + Psi h], y' = phi'0 + phi' h'. General form 4.15 uses beta (biases/offsets) and Omega (weight grids), subscript = layer read from: h_{k+1} = a[beta_k + Omega_k h_k]; output has no ReLU. 4.15 is a CHAIN, not a sum over k: each step's output feeds the next and intermediate lists are discarded. The only summation is inside each matrix-vector product, over the previous layer's units. Matrices never multiply each other here - the ReLU between steps prevents merging them (without it Omega2*Omega1*Omega0 would collapse to one linear map). Bold h_k means a whole layer, unlike h_k in Ch 3 / eqs 4.7-4.9, which meant one unit.
Matrix sizes: rows = units in the layer being fed, columns = units in the layer read from; each bias vector is as long as the layer it feeds. Figure 4.6 (3 inputs, layers 4, 2, 3, 2 outputs): Omega sizes 4x3, 2x4, 3x2, 2x3 = 32 weights + 11 biases = 43 knobs. 4.16 nests every step - read from the innermost bracket out. Why matrices: notation does not grow with width, and GPUs (NVIDIA Tensor Cores) are built for matrix multiplication - most of a network's compute is the Omega x h step.

Figure 4.7: x-axis = number of parameters (cost); y-axis = maximum number of linear regions, log scale (each gridline 100x). Each curve fixes depth K; each dot adds one unit per layer. Shallow: pieces = D + 1; deep: (D + 1)^K. At ~480 knobs: K=1 (159 units) ~160 pieces; K=2 (19 units) 400; K=3 (14) 3,375; K=4 (11) 20,736; K=5 (10 units, 471 knobs = 20 + 4*110 + 11) 161,051. Panel (b), 10 inputs: hinges become flat cuts through 10-D space that intersect in far more ways (3 points cut a line into 4; 3 lines cut a plane into up to 7); K=5, D=50 -> 10,801 knobs, >10^40 regions. Caveats: these are maxima; deep pieces are folded copies, not independent.

Images as input (4.5.4): an image becomes a list of brightness numbers (0-255, scaled to 0-1; 3 per pixel for colour), unrolled row by row. 1,000x1,000 grayscale = 10^6 inputs; with 1,000 first-layer units that is 10^9 weights (~4 GB) - prohibitive. Unrolling also hides neighbours (pixel above/below lands a row-length away), and each position has its own weights, so an object must be relearned at every position (a 10x10 eye has ~982,000 positions in a 10^6-pixel image). Fix: a small 3x3 detector (10 knobs) slid over every position and reused; stacked layers see wider areas - local-to-global (Ch 10).
Receptive field: windows stay 3x3 at every layer, but layer 2 reads layer-1 answers, so it covers 5x5 original pixels, layer 3 7x7 (+2 per layer; 21x21 at layer 10). Downsampling (e.g. keep the max of each 2x2 block) halves the grid so the same window covers twice the original area - like GIS map pyramids / zoom levels. Typical 224x224 network: grid shrinks 224 -> 112 -> 28 -> 7 while detector types grow 3 -> 64 -> 256 -> 512 (edges -> textures -> parts) - a tidy story, messier in reality.

Over-parameterised models (4.5.5): more knobs than training examples (e.g. ~25 million knobs on ~1.3 million images). Each example is one condition, each knob one freedom: 2 points + 2 knobs = one line; 3 points + 2 knobs = compromise; 3 points + 10 knobs = endless perfect fits - so classical statistics predicts memorising noise (overfitting). Observed: training gets easier (many roughly equivalent good solutions, like parking in an empty lot), and deep over-parameterised networks still generalise surprisingly well - not fully understood (Ch 8, Ch 20). Very deep networks become hard to train again (Ch 11, residual networks).

questions.question: In plain words, what does it mean for the first layer to 'fold' the input, and why does stacking a second layer multiply the number of straight pieces rather than adding to it?
questions.answer: The input is divided into segments of equal length by the joints; each segment's y value is the second layer's input, so the second layer 'multiplies the learned activation function' to give the output.
questions.feedback: Partly right: joints split x into stretches and the first layer's output feeds the second. Missing the key idea: the stretches all map onto the SAME output range, so different inputs land on top of each other - that overlap is the fold. The second layer draws one pattern over that shared range, so the pattern is copied once per stretch (mirrored for backward stretches): 3 stretches x 3-piece pattern = 9 pieces. The piece COUNT multiplies; the second layer does not multiply anything. Stretches need not be equal length - training places the joints.

questions.question: With a budget of about 500 knobs, 1 input and 1 output: Option A is one hidden layer of ~160 units; Option B is 5 hidden layers of 10 units. Which can make more straight pieces (roughly how many each), and why might B's extra pieces not help on a particular dataset?
questions.answer: B ~161,000 regions vs A ~160; B's regions are not all independent, so not all are useful.
questions.feedback: Correct (A has ~160 pieces, not units). B's pieces are folded copies of a few patterns, so they only help if the data has that kind of repeated structure; for 160 unrelated wiggles, A's free pieces may fit better.

gaps.text: Folding means the first layer maps several input stretches onto the same output range (overlap); the second layer's pattern is then copied once per stretch, so piece counts multiply. Craig described segments as equal-length and the second layer as 'multiplying'.

questions.question: You tick a dark-mode toggle on a settings screen. Is that client state or server state, and why does the answer decide whether caching rules apply?
questions.answer: Said it could be either: if the setting is saved to the user's account it is server state, and then caching rules apply. Reasoned that you would read the saved value from cache before toggling.
questions.feedback: Classification is right: it depends on who owns the data. A toggle that lives only on this screen is client state; a toggle saved to the account is server state. Refinement: caching rules apply not because you read the cache before toggling, but because the screen shows a copy that can drift from the truth (for example, you switch to dark mode on your phone and the laptop still shows light).

questions.question: You like a post. Which parts of the screen update optimistically, and which other cached views would you refetch instead, and why the different treatment?
questions.answer: Said the liked status and the likes count both update optimistically. Could not name any other cached views to refetch.
questions.feedback: Optimistic half is right. Missing half: a write often affects other cached views of the same data, such as the same post in the feed versus its detail page, a 'posts I liked' list, or the author's total-likes figure. For those, guessing the new content is hard (ordering, paging) and a wrong guess is costly, while a short delay is invisible because they are not on screen. So you mark them stale and refetch them honestly.

gaps.text: Could not name the other cached views affected by a write (feed copy, detail page, 'liked posts' list, author totals) or explain why those are refetched rather than updated optimistically.

Blurred optimistic update and invalidate-on-mutation: both start from a known write, but optimistic writes a guessed new value into the screen, while invalidate asks the server for the true value without guessing.

payload.notes: Prior gap g61-1 (client state conflated with server-side caching layers) resolved: Craig correctly separated client state from server state and tied caching to server state. Only two questions asked; a third retest question is pending.

questions.question: You change your profile photo in a social app. The new photo shows in the top corner right away. Name two other places that may still show the old photo, and say whether you would update each optimistically or refetch it, and why.
questions.answer: Named the profile page, comments on other people's posts, and the photo in groups where he is admin. Updated the landing view optimistically (it is on screen). Refetched the comments and group views because they are off screen, so there is no visible gain from updating them early, and a wrong guess (server rejects the photo) would be costly.
questions.feedback: Correct. Refinement: the server may resize the image or give it a new web address, so even the on-screen guess is only a local preview until the server's real version replaces it. Off-screen views are best marked stale and refetched when next opened.
